title: Attention Is All You Need
meta: Vaswani et al. · Google Brain / Google Research · NIPS 2017 · arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762
tldr: Before 2017, translation models read a sentence **one word at a time** (RNNs), which is slow and makes far-apart words hard to connect. The Transformer throws out recurrence and uses **only attention**: every word looks at every other word at once. It set new records on English→German (28.4 BLEU) and English→French (41.8 BLEU) while costing less to train than earlier models.

blocks.heading: Background you need
bullets: **Sequence transduction**: turning one sequence into another, like a sentence in English into German.
**RNN (recurrent network)**: reads tokens in order, carrying a memory forward, like reading with your finger on the page. It can't be parallelized across positions.
**Attention**: a weighted look-up. Each word asks a question (**query**), every word offers a label (**key**) and content (**value**), and the answer is a weighted mix of values.
**BLEU**: a 0-100 score of how close a translation is to human references. Higher is better.

blocks.heading: The problem
blocks.text: Recurrent models process positions one after another, so training can't use the GPU's parallelism within a sentence, and a signal between the first and last word has to pass through every step in between. Earlier models used attention as an add-on to an RNN. The question here: **can attention alone do the whole job?**

blocks.heading: What they did
bullets: **Encoder-decoder built only from attention and feed-forward layers**: 6 encoder layers and 6 decoder layers, each sublayer wrapped in a residual connection and layer normalization.
**Scaled dot-product attention**: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QKᵀ / √d_k) V. Dividing by √d_k keeps the scores from growing too large.
**Multi-head attention**: 8 heads attend in parallel, each with 64-dimensional keys and values, so the model can look for different kinds of relationships at once.
**Positional encoding**: with no recurrence, word order is added back as sine and cosine waves of different frequencies.
**Base model sizes**: d_model = 512, feed-forward d_ff = 2048, dropout 0.1, label smoothing 0.1.

blocks.caption: Figure 1. The Transformer architecture, drawn from the paper's Figure 1 and Section 3. The decoder's encoder-decoder attention takes queries (Q) from the decoder and keys and values (K, V) from the encoder output.

blocks.heading: Key findings
bullets: **New state of the art, English→German**: the big Transformer scores 28.4 BLEU, more than 2.0 BLEU above the best previous models, including ensembles.
**English→French**: 41.8 BLEU for a single big model, above every model and ensemble in Table 2.
**Cheaper to train**: the base model costs 3.3·10¹⁸ FLOPs, the lowest in Table 2, and still beats every earlier English→German result with 27.3 BLEU.
**Fast**: the base model trains in about 12 hours and the big model in 3.5 days, on one machine with 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs.
**Why attention helps (Table 1)**: any two positions are connected in O(1) steps, versus O(n) for a recurrent layer, with O(1) sequential operations, so a whole sentence is processed in parallel.

blocks.caption: Figure 2. Table 2 of the paper on newstest2014. (a) English→German BLEU. (b) English→German BLEU against training cost. Both Transformers sit above every earlier model at equal or lower cost. (c) English→French BLEU.

blocks.heading: Limitations
bullets: Self-attention costs O(n²·d) per layer, which grows quickly for very long sequences. Section 4 suggests restricting attention to a local neighborhood, which the authors leave to future work.
Evaluated on machine translation and English constituency parsing only.
The base model is behind earlier ensembles on English→French (38.1 vs 41.29 BLEU). Only the big model leads there.

blocks.heading: Why it matters
blocks.text: This paper introduced the architecture behind nearly every modern language model. Replacing step-by-step recurrence with **parallel attention** made training on huge datasets practical, which is the foundation of today's large language models and of vision-language-action models in robotics.
